understanding.does: You sell a post-quantum cryptographic verification layer to institutions and developers who need to verify transactions before settlement, without changing existing infrastructure.
understanding.standsOut: You are betting on being the dedicated verification layer that sits between intent and settlement across every existing network.

constraint.text: No organisation has used QuFi and got a result yet.

evidence: All performance figures are labelled 'target' or 'goal', not measured results.
200+ organisations described as 'in pipeline', not as customers or live integrations.
No price, sign-up, or onboarding path exists for any of the three named products.
The conclusion page lists 'next steps' including 'expand network participation' and 'deploy enterprise solutions', confirming nothing is deployed yet.

tensions: You sell a live verification network. Your site and every page on it show only architecture diagrams, target metrics, and a pipeline of unnamed organisations. No page shows the network running, a verification completing, or a system integrated. | This means a developer or enterprise buyer cannot tell whether QuFi is a working product or a well-documented proposal, so the technical depth of the site does the opposite of what it intends.

You present three named products and invite visitors to explore them. None of the three has a price, a sign-up, a demo request, or any step that moves a visitor toward using or paying for anything. | This means the site functions as a technical whitepaper, not a commercial product, so you are relying entirely on direct outreach to convert the institutional interest the site is designed to generate.

You speak to enterprise compliance teams, blockchain developers and individual node operators in the same pages with the same depth. No part of the site tells any one of them that they are the person you are building this for first. | This means each of the three audiences has to read through material written for the other two to find what is relevant to them, and none of them gets a clear signal that QuFi is built for their specific problem.
unanswered: Is any part of the network live and processing real verifications today, or is everything still pre-launch?
Which of QuVault, QuSettle and QuFi Verify is the primary commercial product versus a protocol component.
Whether any of the three applications is available to buy, license or integrate today, or all are still being built.

The mid-tier European bank is not a cold prospect or a logo on a slide. conversation:
BB: I have read everything you gave me on QuFi Network. One thing stands out before we talk: you have built a complete institutional narrative, a technical architecture, and three named products, but the site gives no visitor anywhere to go next.
The 200+ pipeline claim is your strongest social proof, yet not one name or outcome appears anywhere.
QuVault, QuSettle and QuFi Verify each have an 'Explore' page but no price, no demo request, and no next step, so the site reads as a whitepaper, not a product.
You are speaking to enterprise compliance teams, blockchain developers and node operators in the same breath, which means none of them feels like the person you are building this for first.
Whether any part of the network is live today, or everything is still pre-launch.
What is actually running right now?

FOUNDER: The bank's security team will run an end-to-end verification of a real 
transaction flow: they submit a transaction, our node verifies it, and 
they receive a signed proof they can validate independently. If they 
can reproduce that on their own infrastructure without our engineers 
on the call, we've passed.

BB: That test is a smart line to draw: if they can reproduce the proof without you on the call, it is genuinely independent verification, not a demo. The 60-day clock makes this concrete. What I still cannot see from the site is which of the three products, QuVault, QuSettle or QuFi Verify, is actually what the bank is testing against, because the site presents all three as peers.

Which of the three is the bank running against, and is that the one you consider your primary commercial product right now?

FOUNDER: API references exist. QPL onboarding is partial — a developer can read 
it but needs our team for the first setup. Environment setup is 
manual today. All three would need to be tightened before a bank's 
team can run solo. That's the real work of the next 60 days.

BB: So the 60-day goal is not 'build the product' but 'remove yourself from the setup process', that is a meaningfully different problem. The bank cannot validate independence if your engineers are still required to get the environment running. That also tells me the three products are not really separate commercial choices right now: they are one integrated flow, and the bottleneck is the onboarding layer sitting in front of all three.

Here is what I still need to understand: is this bank already inside the 200+ pipeline you mention on the site, or is it a separate, more advanced relationship that is ahead of everything else?

FOUNDER: Both. Two of the warm contacts are actively waiting for the testnet 
date — they've asked us twice. The rest are warm introductions that 
went quiet. The 60-day clock is real for the two active ones; for the 
rest, we need the testnet live before they re-engage.

goal.confirmed: Signed pilot with the bank in 60 days.

mirror.founderWords: Tighten API references, QPL onboarding and environment setup so a bank's security team can run solo across all three products within 60 days.
mirror.against: API references exist but QPL onboarding is partial and environment setup is manual today, a developer can read the docs but needs the team for first setup.
mirror.tension: You need the bank's team to run solo, but right now no one gets through first setup without you on the call.

strategy.bet: Make the testnet runnable solo by a bank's security team before you do anything else
strategy.over: Reaching new institutions or expanding the pipeline
tradeOffs: The two contacts who asked twice are the fastest path to a signed pilot. Reaching new people before the testnet works solo means everyone hits the same wall.
A guided demo does not give a security team what they need to sign off internally. They need to break it themselves and trust what they find.
The site and the pipeline are not what is blocking the pilot. The manual setup step is. Fix the thing that is actually in the way.
notNow: Leave the quiet pipeline alone for now. They said they will re-engage when the testnet is live, so the testnet being live is the only thing that moves them.
Set the site aside for 60 days. The two contacts who matter already know you, and fixing the copy does not get them to a signed pilot any faster.
You have three products and none of them has a working self-serve path yet. Adding more before the first one is testable solo makes the problem bigger, not smaller.
reconsider: If either warm contact goes cold or says they are no longer waiting, the bet shifts and you need to decide whether to accelerate outreach to the quiet pipeline or find a different first bank.
If the QPL onboarding and environment setup gaps turn out to need more than 60 days to close, the timeline breaks and you need to negotiate a new date with the two contacts before they lose patience.
If the bank's security team runs the test solo and does not move toward a pilot, the assumption that a self-serve test is enough to trigger an internal recommendation needs to be revisited.

week.whyNow: Your two warm contacts have already asked twice for a testnet date. You cannot give them one until you know precisely which steps stop a bank security engineer cold.

today.move: Walk the QPL onboarding flow and write down every step that requires your team.
today.detail: Go through the current environment setup as if you are a bank security engineer working alone. Write down each point where that person would stop and need help, and note why it breaks without someone from QuFi present.

week.doneLooksLike: A written list of every step that currently requires a team member, each with a note on why it breaks without help.

email.subject: Testnet date and what your team will run
email.body:
Hi [Name],

We are getting the testnet environment ready for your security team to run solo, no hand-holding from us required.

Before we send you the date and the runbook, we want to make sure we have mapped every step your engineers will actually hit. That means the QPL onboarding flow, the environment setup, and anything in between where someone would normally have to call us.

Can you tell us: when your security engineers set up a new network environment, where do they usually get stuck? A config step, a credential handoff, a missing dependency, anything like that.

That is the only thing we need from you right now. Once we have it, we will close those gaps, and we will send you the testnet date and a full runbook your team can follow start to finish on their own. You will get a clear proof of what the network does, no sales call attached.

Reply here and we will take it from there.

[Your name]
